content.text: The development of AI technology requires significant infrastructure investments. This includes specialized data centers and high-performance computing components. Companies are making substantial investments to build these capabilities and support the growing demand for AI processing power.

On September 17, 2026, CoreWeave announced the commencement of a Convertible Notes Offering. This offering was initially planned for a $3.0 billion aggregate principal amount of Notes. The company later upsized the offering from this previously announced amount.

The initial conversion price for these notes represented a premium of approximately 22.50%. This premium was calculated over the last reported sale price of $79.88 per share of CoreWeave’s Class A common stock. This stock traded on the Nasdaq Global Select Market on September 17, 2026, the same day the offering was announced.
Cloud Provider Investment Boom

The development of artificial intelligence models requires substantial computing power. This demand drives large investments by major cloud service providers into infrastructure. These companies are increasing their capital expenditures to build out the necessary data centers and acquire specialized hardware.

Microsoft Corp. reported additions to property and equipment of $115,948 million for the fiscal year ended June 30, 2026. This figure compares to $64,551 million for the fiscal year ended June 30, 2025, and $44,477 million for the fiscal year ended June 30, 2024. These investments support growing customer demand for AI infrastructure.

Alphabet reported purchases of property and equipment of $91,447 million for the year ended December 31, 2025. This compares to purchases of property and equipment of $52,535 million for 2024 and purchases of property and equipment of $32,251 million for 2023, reflecting a trend of rising investment.

Amazon's purchases of property and equipment reached $131,819 million for the year ended December 31, 2025. This compares to $82,999 million for 2024 and $52,729 million for 2023. These capital outlays contribute to the expansion of cloud computing capabilities.

Meta's purchases of property and equipment were $69,691 million for the year ended December 31, 2025. This represents purchases of property and equipment of $37,256 million for 2024 and purchases of property and equipment of $27,045 million for 2023. Oracle also showed a substantial increase in capital expenditures.

Oracle reported capital expenditures of $55,663 million for the fiscal year ended May 31, 2026. This was a significant jump from $21,215 million for the fiscal year ended May 31, 2025, and $6,866 million for the fiscal year ended May 31, 2024. These investments are directed toward data center expansion.

Microsoft reported that cost of revenue in its Intelligent Cloud segment increased by $17.7 billion, or 44%, in the fiscal year ended June 30, 2026. This increase was driven by investments in AI infrastructure to support growing customer demand.

In addition to direct capital expenditures, cloud providers also commit to future lease obligations. As of June 30, 2026, Microsoft had additional leases, primarily for data centers, that had not yet commenced. These leases totaled $329.1 billion, with terms ranging from 1 year to 20 years.

Oracle also had substantial off-balance sheet lease commitments. As of May 31, 2026, Oracle had $260 billion of additional lease commitments. These were substantially all related to data center arrangements, with terms of fifteen to nineteen years.
CoreWeave's Business Model

CoreWeave, Inc. operates by providing specialized computing power, primarily for artificial intelligence workloads. The company structures its customer agreements as committed contracts, which typically range from one to six years in their initial period. These contracts are often take-or-pay agreements, meaning customers are required to make payments irrespective of their actual usage of the computing resources.

Customers under these committed contracts frequently make prepayments. These prepayments are initially recorded as deferred revenue on the company's financial statements. The deferred revenue is then recognized as revenue over time, based on the specific terms outlined in each contract.

For the fiscal year ended December 31, 2025, CoreWeave, Inc. reported revenue of $5.1 billion. This represents an increase from the $1.9 billion in revenue reported for the fiscal year ended December 31, 2024. Despite the revenue growth, the company reported a net loss of $1.2 billion for the fiscal year ended December 31, 2025, following a net loss of $863 million for the fiscal year ended December 31, 2024.

The company's operating performance also shifted, with an operating loss of $46 million for the fiscal year ended December 31, 2025, compared to operating income of $324 million for the fiscal year ended December 31, 2024. Research and development expense was $352 million for the fiscal year ended December 31, 2025, an increase from $56 million for the fiscal year ended December 31, 2024.

CoreWeave, Inc. makes significant investments in its infrastructure. Capital expenditures, which represent purchases of property, plant, and equipment, amounted to $10.3 billion for the fiscal year ended December 31, 2025. This followed capital expenditures of $8.7 billion for the fiscal year ended December 31, 2024.

The company's financial position as of December 31, 2025, included cash and cash equivalents of $3.1 billion, an increase from $1.4 billion as of December 31, 2024. Long-term debt, excluding the current portion, also grew to $14.7 billion as of December 31, 2025, from $5.5 billion as of December 31, 2024.
NVIDIA's Role

NVIDIA CORP is a key supplier in the AI infrastructure sector. The company designs and sells graphics processing units, or GPUs, which are essential components for training and running complex AI models. These GPUs enable the parallel processing capabilities required for large-scale AI computations.

The demand for advanced computing hardware from companies building AI infrastructure has driven significant financial results for NVIDIA CORP. For the fiscal year ended January 26, 2025, the company reported revenue of $130.5 billion. Its operating income for that period was $81.5 billion, and net income reached $72.9 billion.

The company's financial performance continued to grow. For the fiscal year ended January 25, 2026, NVIDIA CORP reported revenue of $215.9 billion. Operating income for that fiscal year was $130.4 billion, with net income totaling $120.1 billion.

NVIDIA CORP invests substantially in developing new technologies. Research and development expense was $12.9 billion for the fiscal year ended January 26, 2025. This investment increased to $18.5 billion for the fiscal year ended January 25, 2026, supporting ongoing innovation in its product offerings.

Asset Lives and Depreciation

Cloud computing providers invest heavily in servers and networking equipment. These assets are expensive and have a finite useful life. Companies account for the cost of these assets over their useful lives through depreciation expense.

The estimated useful life of an asset is an accounting judgment. A change in this estimate can significantly impact a company's reported financial results. Different companies use different estimated useful lives for similar assets.

items: Microsoft's 10-K for the fiscal year ended June 30, 2026, states a two to six year estimated useful life for servers and network equipment.
Oracle's 10-K for the fiscal year ended May 31, 2026, states a six-year estimated useful life for servers and networking equipment.
Alphabet's 10-K for 2025 states that it depreciates servers and network equipment generally over a period of six years.

content.text: Amazon changed its estimate of the useful lives of a subset of its servers and networking equipment from six years to five years, effective January 1, 2025. This change was attributed to the increased pace of technology development, particularly in artificial intelligence and machine learning.
Amazon reported that this change in estimate increased depreciation and amortization expense by $1.4 billion and reduced net income by $1.0 billion for the year ended December 31, 2025.

In contrast, Meta increased the estimated useful lives of most of its servers and network assets to 5.5 years, effective January 1, 2025. This change reduced depreciation expense by $2.92 billion and increased net income by $2.59 billion for the year ended December 31, 2025.
CoreWeave also made an adjustment, changing its estimate of the useful life of the computing equipment used in its data centers from five to six years, effective January 1, 2023.
Lessons from Infrastructure

Businesses that provide the underlying infrastructure for new technologies often experience significant demand. As innovation accelerates, the need for foundational components can outpace initial expectations. This dynamic creates opportunities for companies focused on building and maintaining these essential systems.

The rapid evolution of technology can lead to substantial capital expenditures for infrastructure providers. Investing in cutting-edge equipment is crucial to remain competitive and meet the growing processing requirements of advanced applications. These investments are often substantial.

Infrastructure businesses typically involve managing significant fixed assets. The lifespan of these assets, and how their value decreases over time through depreciation, is a key consideration. Understanding these financial aspects is important for assessing the long-term viability of such operations.

The estimated useful life of an asset is a key factor in calculating this expense.

The estimated useful life represents the period over which an asset is expected to generate economic benefits for the company. When a company changes its estimate for an asset's useful life, it directly impacts the amount of depreciation expense recognized in its financial statements. This adjustment can affect both reported expenses and net income.

For the year ended December 31, 2025, Amazon changed its estimate for the useful lives of a subset of its servers and networking equipment. The estimated useful life was adjusted from six years to five years, effective January 1, 2025. This change was attributed to the increased pace of technology development, particularly in artificial intelligence and machine learning.

This adjustment by Amazon resulted in an increase in depreciation and amortization expense by $1.4 billion for the year ended December 31, 2025. Consequently, the company's net income was reduced by $1.0 billion for that same period. Such changes highlight the financial impact of evolving technology on cloud infrastructure providers.

In contrast, Meta increased the estimated useful lives for most of its servers and network assets to 5.5 years, effective January 1, 2025. This change had the effect of reducing depreciation expense by $2.92 billion for the year ended December 31, 2025. The company's net income for that year increased by $2.59 billion as a result of this estimate revision.

Long-Term Compute Contracts

Cloud computing providers often structure their services through committed contracts. These agreements establish a set period during which customers commit to using a certain amount of computing resources.

CoreWeave's 10-K for 2025 indicated that the initial period for its committed contracts typically ranges from one to six years. This structure provides a degree of revenue predictability for cloud infrastructure companies.
These committed contracts are generally take-or-pay agreements. This means customers are required to make payments regardless of how much of the contracted computing capacity they actually utilize.

The take-or-pay nature of these contracts shifts some of the utilization risk from the cloud provider to the customer. This can be beneficial for providers as it helps ensure a steady revenue stream even if a customer's demand fluctuates.

For customers, these contracts can offer predictable pricing and guaranteed access to computing resources. However, they also require careful forecasting of their compute needs to avoid paying for unused capacity.
Lessons from Cloud Infrastructure

The evolution of cloud infrastructure highlights the importance of capital expenditures in driving business growth. Businesses that require substantial investment in physical assets often face high fixed costs. These costs must be managed carefully to ensure profitability as demand for services fluctuates over time.

The scale of operations in the cloud sector also demonstrates how large infrastructure projects can create significant barriers to entry for new competitors. Building and maintaining a global network of data centers demands considerable resources and specialized expertise, which are not easily replicated by new entrants.

content.text: On September 10, 2026, an Underwriting Agreement was established involving Vistra Operations, Vistra, and a group of underwriters. The underwriters included Barclays Capital Inc., BofA Securities, Inc., Mizuho Securities USA LLC, MUFG Securities Americas Inc., and Truist Securities, Inc. These entities acted as representatives for other underwriters listed in Schedule A of the agreement.

This agreement detailed the terms for the sale of specific Securities. It outlined how these financial instruments were offered to investors. Such agreements are a standard part of bringing new securities to public markets, defining the roles and responsibilities of the parties involved in the offering process.
Data Center Energy History

Electricity consumption by data centers has seen varied growth over time. The Department of Energy reported that total data center electricity usage increased from 58 TWh in 2014 to 176 TWh in 2023. This expansion reflects the evolving demands of digital infrastructure.

A report from the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory estimated that data center electricity use remained stable at approximately 60 TWh between 2014 and 2016. This period of stability preceded a notable shift in energy consumption patterns.

In 2017, GPU-accelerated servers, used for artificial intelligence, became a significant part of the data center server stock. This development marked a turning point, as total data center electricity use began to increase again after the period of stability.

The report estimated that data centers consumed about 76 TWh in 2018. This amount represented 1.9% of total U.S. electricity consumption for that year, highlighting the growing energy footprint of these facilities.

The composition of data center types also shifted. Internal data centers accounted for over 60% of server energy consumption in 2014. By 2023, their share of server energy consumption decreased to nearly 10%.

Conversely, hyperscale and colocation data centers grew in prominence. These larger facilities accounted for almost 80% of server energy consumption in 2023. This change reflects a consolidation and specialization within the data center industry.
Demand for Data Centers

Data centers are facilities that house computer servers and related equipment. These centers require significant amounts of electricity to power their operations and to cool the equipment within them. The power consumption of data centers has become a notable aspect of overall electricity demand.

The Department of Energy describes data centers as one of the most energy-intensive building types. These facilities consume 10 to 50 times the energy per floor space of a typical commercial office building. This intensive energy use is due to the continuous operation and cooling needs of the computing infrastructure.

A December 2024 Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory report provided estimates on U.S. data center electricity consumption. The report estimated that U.S. data centers consumed 176 TWh of electricity in 2023. This amount represented 4.4% of total U.S. electricity consumption for that year.
Grid Interconnection Queues

Connecting new power generation facilities to the existing transmission system is a detailed process. The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, or FERC, regulates these procedures and agreements. This process is essential for any new power source, including those that would supply electricity to data centers, which require substantial and reliable electricity.

As of the end of 2022, over 10,000 active interconnection requests were in queues across the United States. These requests represented more than 2,000 gigawatts of potential generation and storage capacity. The volume of requests indicates significant interest in expanding power infrastructure.
The interconnection process has faced delays. Of the 2,179 interconnection studies completed in 2022, 68% were issued late. These delays can affect the timeline for bringing new power sources online.

To address these challenges, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission issued Order No. 2023. This order reforms the procedures and agreements that transmission providers use to connect new generating facilities to the transmission system. It aims to streamline the process and reduce delays.

Order No. 2023 requires transmission providers to replace the serial first-come, first-served study process with a first-ready, first-served cluster study process. This new approach studies proposed generating facilities in batches, which can make the process more efficient.

Interconnection customers also have new requirements under Order No. 2023. They must demonstrate 90% site control when submitting an interconnection request. They also need to show 100% site control when executing the facilities study agreement. These requirements aim to ensure projects are ready for development.

The order introduced penalties to encourage compliance. Transmission providers that miss study deadlines face penalties. Similarly, interconnection customers whose withdrawal materially affects the cost or timing of other requests with an equal or lower queue position also face withdrawal penalties.

Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory reported that as of the end of 2025, approximately 8,200 projects were actively seeking grid interconnection in the U.S. These projects represented 1,312 gigawatts of generation and about 749 gigawatts of storage capacity.

The laboratory also reported on the lengthy timelines involved. The median project built in 2025 took 61 months from the initial interconnection request to achieving commercial operation. This extended period highlights the time investment required for new power sources.

Furthermore, the laboratory’s data showed that only 13% of the capacity that submitted interconnection requests from 2000 to 2020 had reached commercial operation by the end of 2025. In contrast, 75% of these requests had been withdrawn, and 10% remained active.

The laboratory also noted a significant increase in active natural gas capacity in interconnection queues. This capacity increased 86% in 2025, reaching 253 gigawatts. This indicates a growing interest in natural gas as a power source.

Data center operators need reliable and substantial power supplies. To secure these, companies like Microsoft, Meta Platforms, and Amazon Web Services enter into power purchase agreements with energy providers such as Constellation and Vistra. These agreements outline the terms for purchasing electricity over an extended period.

The terms of a power purchase agreement can vary. In September 2024, Constellation executed a 20-year power purchase agreement with Microsoft. This agreement supports the restart of Three Mile Island Unit 1, which was renamed the Crane Clean Energy Center.

content.text: Another instance occurred in June 2025, when Constellation signed a 20-year power purchase agreement with Meta Platforms. This agreement covers the output of the Clinton Clean Energy Center and is set to begin in June 2027.

Vistra has also engaged in significant power purchase agreements to supply carbon-free power to technology companies. In September 2025, Vistra announced a 20-year power purchase agreement with Amazon Web Services. This agreement includes options to extend for up to an additional 20 years.

Under the agreement, Vistra is to supply Amazon Web Services with 1,200 MW of carbon-free power from its Comanche Peak Nuclear Power Plant. This demonstrates the scale of power needed by data centers.

In January 2026, Vistra announced further 20-year power purchase agreements with Meta Platforms. These agreements involve supplying 2,609 MW of carbon-free power and capacity from its PJM nuclear plants. This includes 2,176 MW of operating energy and capacity, along with 433 MW of uprate energy and capacity to be constructed.

Power purchase agreements expose energy providers to credit risk. This is the risk that counterparties may not fulfill their obligations under the agreement. Energy providers manage this through hedging, risk management, and the terms of these agreements.
Nuclear Plant Renewals

Nuclear power plants operate under licenses issued by the Nuclear Regulatory Commission. Each license is for a fixed period. Under 10 CFR 50.51, this period cannot exceed 40 years from the original issuance date. This rule applies to most licenses, with exceptions for certain non-power production or utilization facility licenses issued after January 29, 2025.

These operating licenses can be renewed. Under 10 CFR 54.31, a renewed license is granted for the remaining years of the current license term. An additional period of not more than 20 years is then added. The total duration of a renewed license may not exceed 40 years. A renewed license also has the potential to be renewed again.
Lessons for Investors

The growth of data centers illustrates how technological advancements can create ripple effects across various sectors. The need for advanced computing often drives significant infrastructure development. This development, in turn, can place new demands on existing resources and supply chains, leading to both opportunities and challenges for many market participants.

Understanding how different industries adapt to evolving technological landscapes is important for investors. The increasing power requirements for data centers highlight the critical role of utility companies and energy infrastructure. Recognizing these interdependencies can provide insights into potential areas for growth and areas that may require substantial investment.

The process of connecting new power sources to the electrical grid, as seen with data centers, can be complex. It involves careful planning and coordination to ensure reliability and capacity. This complexity can affect the timelines and costs associated with bringing new projects online, which is a factor that industries relying on such infrastructure consider.

Long-term agreements, such as power purchase agreements, demonstrate how businesses seek to secure essential resources. These agreements can provide stability for both the energy consumer and the energy producer. They also reflect efforts to manage future costs and ensure a consistent supply of power, which is vital for continuous operations.

sections.title: The Rise of Specialized AI Infrastructure

content.text: The emergence of artificial intelligence models created a need for advanced computing infrastructure. Traditional data centers, which were designed for general-purpose computing tasks, often lacked the specific processing power and architecture required to efficiently train and deploy complex AI models. This disparity opened a path for new types of infrastructure solutions.

The development of specialized AI infrastructure involves substantial capital outlays. Building data centers specifically equipped for high-performance computing, essential for AI workloads, demands significant investment. This funding supports the acquisition of specialized hardware components, advanced cooling systems, and robust power delivery mechanisms necessary for operating intensive AI computations reliably.
Specialized Providers

Companies focused on providing AI-optimized cloud computing services began to emerge. These providers concentrate on offering infrastructure tailored for machine learning and AI tasks. Their systems are built to handle the demanding processing requirements associated with both the training and ongoing operation of large-scale AI models.

CoreWeave, Inc. is an example of a company that has developed specialized infrastructure for AI. This company's offerings are designed to meet the unique computing needs of AI developers and researchers. Such specialized providers offer an alternative to general cloud services for clients with intense AI workloads.

The operational structure for these specialized services often includes committed contracts. CoreWeave's 10-K for 2025 states that the initial period for its committed contracts typically ranges from one to six years. These agreements are generally structured as take-or-pay, meaning customers are required to make payments regardless of their actual utilization of the compute resources.

Under these committed contracts, customers often provide a prepayment. This prepayment is recorded as deferred revenue by the provider. The deferred revenue is then recognized over time as the services are consumed, according to the terms specified in the contract. This model helps secure revenue streams for the infrastructure providers.

The scale of investment in this sector is illustrated by financial reports. CoreWeave, Inc. reported capital expenditures for purchases of property, plant, and equipment of $8.7 billion for the fiscal year ended December 31, 2024. This figure increased to $10.3 billion for the fiscal year ended December 31, 2025.

Revenue growth for specialized providers also reflects the increasing demand for AI infrastructure. CoreWeave, Inc. reported revenue of $1.9 billion for the fiscal year ended December 31, 2024. This revenue grew to $5.1 billion for the fiscal year ended December 31, 2025, indicating significant expansion in the market.

Cloud providers are major investors in the infrastructure supporting AI. These companies operate vast networks of data centers, which house the specialized hardware required for AI model training and inference. The significant capital expenditures involved reflect the scale of this investment.

Microsoft's capital expenditures, for example, demonstrate this trend. The company reported additions to property and equipment of $115,948 million for the fiscal year ended June 30, 2026. This figure compares with $64,551 million for the fiscal year ended June 30, 2025.

The increase in capital spending by Microsoft also compares to $44,477 million for the fiscal year ended June 30, 2024. This growth in investment underpins the expansion of cloud services that cater to AI workloads.

Other major cloud providers also show substantial capital expenditures. For the year ended December 31, 2025, Alphabet reported purchases of property and equipment of $91,447 million. This compares to purchases of property and equipment of $52,535 million for 2024 and purchases of property and equipment of $32,251 million for 2023.

Amazon's purchases of property and equipment amounted to $131,819 million for the year ended December 31, 2025. This was an increase from purchases of property and equipment of $82,999 million for 2024 and purchases of property and equipment of $52,729 million for 2023.

Meta also showed significant investment, with purchases of property and equipment of $69,691 million for the year ended December 31, 2025. This compares to purchases of property and equipment of $37,256 million for 2024 and purchases of property and equipment of $27,045 million for 2023.

Oracle's capital expenditures for the fiscal year ended May 31, 2026, were $55,663 million. This represents a rise from capital expenditures of $21,215 million for the fiscal year ended May 31, 2025, and capital expenditures of $6,866 million for the fiscal year ended May 31, 2024.
Growing Cloud Demand

The demand for AI infrastructure drives these expenditures. Microsoft reported that the cost of revenue in its Intelligent Cloud segment increased by $17.7 billion, or 44%, in the fiscal year ended June 30, 2026. This increase was attributed to investments in AI infrastructure to support growing customer demand.

Cloud providers not only purchase property and equipment but also enter into significant lease commitments for data centers. These leases represent substantial future obligations for expanding their infrastructure capacity.

As of June 30, 2026, Microsoft had additional leases, primarily for data centers, that had not yet commenced, totaling $329.1 billion. These lease terms range from 1 year to 20 years, indicating long-term commitments to infrastructure.

Similarly, as of May 31, 2026, Oracle had $260 billion of additional lease commitments. These commitments are substantially all related to data center arrangements, with terms ranging from fifteen to nineteen years. Such leases are not immediately reflected on the consolidated balance sheet.

The development and deployment of advanced AI systems rely heavily on specialized hardware. This has created a significant role for hardware providers that design and manufacture the components essential for AI infrastructure. These providers often focus on graphics processing units (GPUs) and other accelerators that can handle the complex computations required for training and running AI models.

NVIDIA CORP is a key hardware provider in this sector. The company reported revenue of $130.5 billion for the fiscal year ended January 26, 2025. This revenue increased to $215.9 billion for the fiscal year ended January 25, 2026. This demonstrates the growing demand for specialized AI hardware.

The profitability of hardware providers is also notable. NVIDIA CORP reported operating income of $81.5 billion for the fiscal year ended January 26, 2025, and $130.4 billion for the fiscal year ended January 25, 2026. Net income was $72.9 billion for the fiscal year ended January 26, 2025, and $120.1 billion for the fiscal year ended January 25, 2026. These figures highlight the economic impact of the AI infrastructure build-out.
Investing in Innovation

Hardware providers must continuously invest in research and development to maintain their competitive edge. The rapid evolution of AI technology requires constant innovation in chip design and manufacturing processes. These investments are crucial for developing more powerful and efficient hardware.

NVIDIA CORP's research and development expense was $12.9 billion for the fiscal year ended January 26, 2025. This expense increased to $18.5 billion for the fiscal year ended January 25, 2026. Capital expenditures, which include purchases of property, equipment, and intangible assets, were $3.2 billion and $6 billion for the respective fiscal years.

The useful life of servers and networking equipment is a significant factor for companies investing in AI infrastructure. This useful life determines how quickly these assets are depreciated on financial statements.

A change in the estimated useful life of an asset can impact a company's reported depreciation and net income. For example, Amazon changed its estimate for a subset of its servers and networking equipment from six years to five years, effective January 1, 2025.

Amazon cited the increased pace of technology development, particularly in artificial intelligence and machine learning, for this change. The change increased depreciation and amortization expense by $1.4 billion and reduced net income by $1.0 billion for the year ended December 31, 2025.

In contrast, Meta increased the estimated useful lives of most of its servers and network assets to 5.5 years, effective January 1, 2025. This change reduced depreciation expense by $2.92 billion and increased net income by $2.59 billion for the year ended December 31, 2025.

Other companies also disclose their depreciation policies. Alphabet's 10-K for 2025 states that it depreciates servers and network equipment generally over a period of six years. Alphabet recognizes any change in estimated useful lives on a prospective basis.

Microsoft's 10-K for the fiscal year ended June 30, 2026, gives an estimated useful life of two to six years for servers and network equipment. Oracle's 10-K for the fiscal year ended May 31, 2026, states that its computer, network, machinery and equipment, primarily servers and networking equipment, have an estimated useful life of six years.
CoreWeave also adjusted its estimate of useful life for computing equipment in its data centers, changing it from five to six years, effective January 1, 2023.

The build-out of new infrastructure often involves substantial capital expenditures. Companies invest heavily in physical assets like data centers, specialized processors, and networking equipment to support new technologies. These investments aim to create the foundation for future growth and service delivery, but they also carry significant financial considerations.

Technological advancements can lead to rapid shifts in demand for different types of infrastructure. Companies must consider the pace of innovation when making long-term investment decisions. The risk of obsolescence is a key factor in such capital-intensive industries, as new generations of technology can quickly render older assets less effective.

content.text: The demand for significant computing power has grown with the expansion of artificial intelligence. This growth requires specialized infrastructure known as AI data centers. These facilities are designed to handle the intensive computational needs of AI models and applications, consuming substantial amounts of electricity.

Energy companies are responding to this increased demand. In September 2025, Vistra announced a 20-year power purchase agreement with Amazon Web Services. This agreement includes options to extend for up to an additional 20 years, to supply 1,200 MW of carbon-free power from its Comanche Peak Nuclear Power Plant.

Following this, in January 2026, Vistra announced 20-year power purchase agreements with Meta Platforms. These agreements involve supplying 2,609 MW of carbon-free power and capacity from Vistra's PJM nuclear plants. This includes 2,176 MW of operating energy and capacity and 433 MW of uprate energy and capacity yet to be constructed.

On September 10, 2026, Vistra Operations and Vistra executed an Underwriting Agreement with several underwriters, including Barclays Capital Inc., BofA Securities, Inc., Mizuho Securities USA LLC, MUFG Securities Americas Inc., and Truist Securities, Inc. This agreement facilitated the sale of securities.

Data centers operate as critical infrastructure, requiring substantial electricity. The Department of Energy describes these facilities as highly energy-intensive. They consume 10 to 50 times more energy per floor space than a standard commercial office building. This high consumption reflects the continuous operation of servers and cooling systems necessary for data processing.

The total electricity usage by US data centers has seen a significant increase over time. In 2014, data centers consumed 58 TWh of electricity. This usage remained fairly stable at about 60 TWh between 2014 and 2016, according to a December 2024 Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory report.

A turning point occurred when GPU-accelerated servers, used for artificial intelligence, became a significant part of the data center server stock in 2017. This development led to a renewed increase in total data center electricity use. By 2018, data centers consumed about 76 TWh, representing 1.9% of total US electricity consumption.

Connecting new power generation facilities to the existing electrical grid presents a complex challenge for data centers. The process involves navigating interconnection queues, which are backlogs of requests from facilities seeking to connect. These queues can delay the deployment of new power sources essential for data center expansion and operation.

As of the end of 2022, over 10,000 active interconnection requests were in queues throughout the United States. These requests represented more than 2,000 gigawatts of potential generation and storage capacity. The volume of requests contributes to extended timelines for grid integration, impacting project development.

The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, or FERC, issued Order No. 2023 on July 28, 2023. This order aimed to reform the procedures and agreements that transmission providers use to connect new generating facilities to the transmission system. It addressed issues within the existing interconnection process.

Data centers require a consistent and substantial power supply. Nuclear power plants can offer a continuous, carbon-free energy source that meets these demands. The long operational period of nuclear facilities aligns with the long-term energy needs of large-scale data center operations.

Nuclear power plant licenses are typically issued for a fixed period. Under 10 CFR 50.51, an initial license cannot exceed 40 years from its issuance date. These licenses can be renewed, extending their operational life.

Power purchase agreements represent a contractual arrangement for the sale and purchase of electricity. These agreements are common in the energy sector, especially for large-scale projects and renewable energy sources. They provide a predictable revenue stream for power generators and a stable energy supply for purchasers.

For data center operators, power purchase agreements offer a way to secure long-term, specific energy sources, including those with carbon-free attributes. This approach helps these operators meet their substantial power demands while aligning with sustainability goals.

content.text: On September 2, 2026, NVIDIA Corporation entered into a definitive agreement to acquire Hugging Face, Inc. This acquisition represents a strategic move in the evolving landscape of artificial intelligence. NVIDIA is a prominent designer of graphics processing units, which are key components for AI development.

Hugging Face operates a platform for machine learning developers, offering tools and models that support the creation and deployment of AI applications. The combination of NVIDIA's hardware capabilities and Hugging Face's software ecosystem could influence future AI infrastructure development.

The foundation of modern artificial intelligence infrastructure rests on the expansion of cloud computing. Large technology companies built vast networks of data centers to offer on-demand computing services, storage, and networking over the internet. This infrastructure supports a wide range of digital services, from streaming video to business applications.

The growth of these cloud platforms required substantial capital investments in property and equipment. Companies like Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, and Oracle have consistently allocated significant financial resources to expand their global data center footprints.
Rising Capital Expenditures

The reported capital expenditures show a trend of increasing investment. For the fiscal year ended June 30, 2024, Microsoft reported additions to property and equipment of $44,477 million. This figure increased to $64,551 million for the fiscal year ended June 30, 2025, and reached $115,948 million for the fiscal year ended June 30, 2026.

Alphabet's purchases of property and equipment were $32,251 million for the year ended December 31, 2023. These purchases rose to $52,535 million for the year ended December 31, 2024, and further to $91,447 million for the year ended December 31, 2025.

Amazon also demonstrated significant capital outlays. The company reported purchases of property and equipment of $52,729 million for the year ended December 31, 2023. This figure grew to purchases of property and equipment of $82,999 million for the year ended December 31, 2024, and reached purchases of property and equipment of $131,819 million for the year ended December 31, 2025.

Meta's investment in property and equipment followed a similar pattern. Purchases were $27,045 million for the year ended December 31, 2023, increasing to $37,256 million for the year ended December 31, 2024, and then to $69,691 million for the year ended December 31, 2025.

Oracle's capital expenditures also showed substantial growth. The company reported $6,866 million for the fiscal year ended May 31, 2024. This expanded to $21,215 million for the fiscal year ended May 31, 2025, and further to $55,663 million for the fiscal year ended May 31, 2026.

These capital expenditures reflect the continuous investment required to build and maintain the global network of data centers that power cloud services and, increasingly, artificial intelligence applications.
Cloud Provider Spending

The demand for AI infrastructure drives significant capital expenditures from major cloud computing providers. These companies invest heavily in property, plant, and equipment, including data centers and specialized hardware.

Microsoft reported additions to property and equipment of $115,948 million for the fiscal year ended June 30, 2026. This compares to $64,551 million for the fiscal year ended June 30, 2025, and $44,477 million for the fiscal year ended June 30, 2024.

The increase in cost of revenue in Microsoft's Intelligent Cloud segment was $17.7 billion, or 44%, in the fiscal year ended June 30, 2026. This increase was due to investments in AI infrastructure to support customer demand.

Alphabet reported purchases of property and equipment of $91,447 million for the year ended December 31, 2025. This compares to $52,535 million for 2024 and $32,251 million for 2023. These investments support the expansion of cloud services and AI capabilities.

Amazon reported purchases of property and equipment of $131,819 million for the year ended December 31, 2025. This figure compares to $82,999 million for 2024 and $52,729 million for 2023. The scale of these expenditures reflects the ongoing build-out of its global infrastructure.

Meta reported purchases of property and equipment of $69,691 million for the year ended December 31, 2025. This compares to $37,256 million for 2024 and $27,045 million for 2023. These expenditures are part of a broader strategy to develop advanced computing environments.

Oracle reported capital expenditures of $55,663 million for the fiscal year ended May 31, 2026. This compares to $21,215 million for the fiscal year ended May 31, 2025, and $6,866 million for the fiscal year ended May 31, 2024. These investments support its cloud offerings.
Vendor Capital Spending

Beyond the cloud computing providers, other companies also contribute to the AI infrastructure spending cycle. NVIDIA CORP reported capital expenditures of $6 billion for the fiscal year ended January 25, 2026.
This figure for NVIDIA CORP represents an increase from $3.2 billion for the fiscal year ended January 26, 2025. These expenditures include property, equipment, and intangible assets.
Broadcom Inc. reported capital expenditures of $623 million for the fiscal year ended November 2, 2025. This compares to $548 million for the fiscal year ended November 3, 2024.
These purchases of property, plant, and equipment by Broadcom Inc. support operations within the broader technology ecosystem.
Future Commitments

Cloud computing providers also make significant long-term commitments for future infrastructure. As of June 30, 2026, Microsoft had additional leases, primarily for datacenters, that had not yet commenced.
These uncommenced leases for Microsoft totaled $329.1 billion, with lease terms ranging from 1 year to 20 years.

The estimated useful life of a server or other computing equipment is an accounting assumption that affects a company's financial reporting. When a company buys an asset, its cost is spread out over its useful life through a process called depreciation. This allows the company to match the expense of the asset with the revenue it helps generate over time.

A shorter estimated useful life means the asset's cost is depreciated over fewer years, leading to a higher annual depreciation expense. This reduces reported net income in the short term. Conversely, a longer estimated useful life results in lower annual depreciation expense and a higher reported net income.

These estimates are particularly important for companies that invest heavily in infrastructure, such as those in the cloud computing and artificial intelligence sectors. The significant capital expenditure on servers and networking equipment makes changes to useful life estimates impactful on financial statements.
Differing Estimates

Different companies use varying estimates for the useful lives of their assets. Impact of Technology

The rapid pace of technological development can influence these useful life estimates. This change reduced Meta's depreciation expense by $2.92 billion and increased net income by $2.59 billion for the year ended December 31, 2025.

Cloud computing providers often structure their agreements with customers through various contract models. A common approach for specialized compute services, particularly in areas such as AI, involves committed contracts. These agreements secure access to computing resources over a defined period.

For example, CoreWeave's committed contracts typically span an initial period ranging from one to six years. These contracts are frequently structured as take-or-pay agreements, meaning the customer is obligated to make payments regardless of their actual usage of the computing resources.

Under a take-or-pay structure, the cloud provider gains revenue predictability, which can support investments in new infrastructure. Customers secure access to high-demand computing capacity, which is crucial for resource-intensive workloads like AI model training.

Customers under committed contracts often make a prepayment. This prepayment is recorded by the provider as deferred revenue. The deferred revenue is then consumed by the customer over the contract term, based on the specific terms agreed upon.

The prevalence of committed contracts can be seen in CoreWeave's revenue composition. For the year ended December 31, 2025, committed contracts accounted for over 98% of CoreWeave's revenue. This compares to 96% for 2024 and 88% for 2023.
